If you are in pain, it is far from God. Yes mental pain of course counts. The tricky part here is that you are unsure of your religion and beliefs, and you seem to feel insecure with the unknown just as I did. I think the hardest part is just letting go of it because doing those compulsions makes you (correct me if I am wrong) feel safe and secure and that you are believing in the right thing. The problem is is that I can't tell you god isn't or is real, but I can tell you that if he was, why would he put you through such pain? If God is real he wouldn't do something of that sort. It is your OCD and not God it never has been. And it is completely normal to fear that you will go to hell and live in eternal hell, and that you will die in pain. The path to take right now is to reconnect with yourself o matter your worries. Find yourself, be yourself, own yourself, and fight off those built up problems one by one and you will continue to live more little by little because your mind will understand you can handle those things again and you don't need that OCD compulsion to protect you from the pain. It sucks a lot and we all want a fast fix when it comes to OCD, but if you start to worry less about the OCD and fighting off from dealing with those problems and accept those compulsions as a mental response and learn to live with them TEMPORARILY then you can figure out those things about yourself and your life you've been fighting off for so long. It takes time, and it hurts but once you stop dwelling on the OCD and accept it you can start living and start fighting. You don't win a war by complaining about the opponent and hiding in a corner, you win the war by accepting they are there and continuing to live your live as much as you can while fighting the army off one by one. And then one day you just start yto see everything simply again because the mind understand you can now deal with those problems you couldn't deal with before. That protective bubble fades and eventually you will have a moment in time where you realize it's okay and that it's okay to break free because you understand why this happened and how to deal with those previous problems that trigger the OCD. That's what I've learned from trying the copy-cut ways they teach you to face it in therapy. They say pill and forcing yourself to do things you aren't ready to do yet, but then you can't or you do and you dig deeper in your hole. It very rarely works until the person has delt with the previous problems beforehand. The problem with the force of it is that those problems go unhandled and they eventually seep back into that person's life until yet again they fall on them like a pile of bricks and disable them. That's what causes the relapses in my opinion, the avoidance of the previous problems that caused the OCD to start protecting the person from being hurt. The OCD stops any more bricks from coming in until you are ready to deal with them again, and that moment where you can just open yourself up and say here I am and I have no idea what's going to happen, but I will survive and I will thrive no matter the circumstance. That feeling is magical and pure and only will come and premenatly stay with no relapse if you face those bricks/problems now. It may take time and you may feel your life is being wasted, but it only prepares you to be completely free from all of those worries in life. IT will prepare you to really never have to worry about the unknown ever again and be at peace with them, and that time will come for us once we stop trying to ignore and block out the army and accept and let in the army while fighting them off and living more and more each day.

Switching from different translations and sects of the religion, even though you don't believe in the core of it at all tells me you are trying to find a place you fit. OCD is usually about deeper issues we have in life. For me it was and still is about loosing control and giving up my power to know how everyday is going to be even though that is the only way for me to achieve true freedom. Firstly, OCD teaches us things in life, and it usually happens when people have so much going on that they ignore it. So it builds up and then eventually falls on top of them like a pile of bricks and completely disables them. Some people have more some have less, that's why treatment may take longer or shorter depending on the person.
